analysis.investment_thesis: Supertech EV fails the Magic Formula decisively: ROE of 0.47% implies near-zero return on capital, so even a superficially cheap P/E of 8.21 is meaningless. A "cheap bad business" is still a bad business — this is the opposite of what the formula seeks.
key_strengths: Optically low P/E of 8.21 suggests headline cheapness
Exposure to a structurally growing EV 2W/3W segment in India
key_risks: ROE of 0.47% signals capital is earning virtually nothing — ROIC almost certainly <5%
Tiny Rs 54 Cr micro-cap incorporated only in 2022 — no operating track record
Brutal competition from Ola, TVS, Bajaj, Ather in 2W EV with thin/negative margins
red_flags: ROE 0.47% — fails Greenblatt's ROIC threshold by an order of magnitude
Zero DII ownership — no institutional validation
Sub-3-year-old company — Magic Formula requires sustained ROIC, impossible to verify here
analysis.detailed_analysis:
From a Magic Formula lens, the two inputs that matter are earnings yield (EBIT/EV) and return on capital. The P/E of 8.21 hints at an earnings yield around 10–12%, which is borderline-attractive on its own. But ROE of 0.47% is catastrophic — a business earning less than half a percent on equity is destroying economic value once you account for any cost of capital. ROIC is almost certainly in low single digits, well below my 20%+ screen. The formula only works when cheap meets good; this is cheap meets terrible.

Additionally, a 2022-incorporated Rs 54 Cr micro-cap in the hyper-competitive Indian EV 2W/3W space has no durable evidence of the high, sustained ROIC the strategy demands. Without positive operating economics to compound, the low P/E is a value trap, not a bargain. I'd skip this and let the screen surface businesses that actually earn high returns on the capital they deploy.
